newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Caretakers reject Bhutto plea for say in IMF loan.
newsitem.headline: Caretakers reject Bhutto plea for say in IMF loan.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government on Monday rejected ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's demand that an agreement on a restructuring loan being negotiated with the IMF be approved by top political parties.

Caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid's cabinet noted Bhutto's demand, made in a letter to President Farooq Leghari, and regarded it as "an extremely reprehensible action which is against national interest", a government minister said after a cabinet meeting.

Information Minister Irshad Haqqani told a news conference that Bhutto's letter sent on Sunday related to Pakistan's vital economic interests and was an attempt to shake the international community's confidence in Pakistan.

"But we do not want to take any punitive action against her (Bhutto)," he said. "The process of accountability is taking its course," he added apparently referring to charges the government is likely to bring against her before an accountability commission.

A letter from Bhutto to Leghari said the caretaker government he installed after dismissing her government earlier this month had no right to negotiate such loans with the International Monetary Fund.

"In any democratic system, long-term pledges on matters of vital economic importance should only be made by a duly elected political government, responsible to the legislature and the people," she wrote.

But Bhutto said if an agreement with the IMF had to be signed in national interest, her the People's Democratic Front (PDF) alliance and the Pakistan Muslim League of her chief political foe, former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, must agree to the conditions for a structural adjustment loan.

Haqqani said Bhutto "has no locus standi to make such demands. Since she has gone to court (to challenge her dismissal), she is in no position to be making demands to the government to enter any agreement or not."
He said the nation would be taken into confidence about the details after the talks between the government and the IMF. "Everything would be transparent and before the nation."

Bhutto's letter stopped short of saying she would disown the deal if the Supreme Court ruled that her government was deposed unconstitutionally, as she has asked it to, or her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won elections scheduled for February.
But in a talk to journalists on Monday in the Punjab province capital of Lahore, she asked: "In case of restoration of my government, what explanation we would offer to the people of Pakistan?"

An IMF mission that visited Pakistan after Bhutto was dismissed on charges of corruption and incompetence, accusations she vehemently denies, agreed to recommend the reactivation of a $600 million standby loan.
The deal, which the IMF board is expected to approve by mid-December, would involve the swift release of two tranches of $80 million to shore up Pakistan's low foreign reserves.
